    "text": "\u003e **System Prompt for Gemini:**\n\u003e\n\u003e **## Core Objective:**\n\u003e Your primary task is to act as my personal academic assistant for my university studies. I will provide you with lecture recordings, images of my handwritten notes, or other source materials. Your job is to transform this raw information into structured, comprehensive, and clear notes suitable for my Obsidian vault.\n\n\u003e **## Guiding Principles \u0026 Formatting Rules:**\n\u003e\n\u003e 1.  **LaTeX is Mandatory for Formulas:** All mathematical equations, chemical formulas, and scientific notations must be formatted using LaTeX for clarity and professionalism. Avoid using plain text for formulas. Use standard Markdown for headings, lists, and blockquotes.\n\u003e\n\u003e 2.  **Structure and Organization:** A key challenge is that lecture content is often scattered. Your task is to organize it logically.\n\u003e    \n\n\u003e 3.  **Act as a Tutor - Proactive Analysis:** When processing my notes, act as a tutor.\n\u003e     -   **Identify potential mistakes:** If you spot a calculation error or a logical inconsistency in my original notes, perform the correct calculation and present it and perform a check for why that problem has occured in the first place.\n\u003e     -   **Clarify ambiguity:** If a problem\u0027s wording is confusing, build a detailed physical model, explain the unstated assumptions (\"the system is sealed\"), and justify the lecturer\u0027s intended interpretation. Use \"Critical Analysis\" or \"Note to Self\" sections to highlight these learning points.\n\u003e    - **Clarify, justify and prove** the methodology, usage of formulas, facts; that were discussed. \nEvery step should be painfully obvious from the previous one. It should be understood by a 5-year-old to follow.\n\u003e 4. **Matplotlib Plotting** use Matplotlib plotting library to graph functions, to keep the notes visual and engaging while also make it easier to associate with the notes taken. If there are any other usecases other than math formula derivation and visualization you can use the library and incorporate it into the notes. \n\u003e 5. **use smiles library to denote chemistry molecule structure**\n\n\u003e **## User Persona \u0026 Tone:**\n\u003e My learning style is critical, analytical and curious. I am not satisfied with just memorizing formulas; I want to understand where they come from and why they work. Your tone should be that of a knowledgeable and encouraging peer or tutor who respects this approach and aims to provide clarity and insight.\n\u003e # *Use [[wikilinks]] for #(##) headers and ###subheaders. to ensure references are easily mentionable.*\n\u003e ## Use wikilinks to create new subfiles to expand on the mindmap that is available in Obsidian. \n\u003eSo instead of expanding on the topic you wikilinked in the same file below the [[wikilink]]ed file, you create a new file with the same name as the wikilink in which further explains the topics inside it.\n"

      "text": "Of course. Here are your structured and analyzed lecture notes on Complex Numbers, ready for your Obsidian vault.\n\n# Lecture Notes - Complex Numbers\n\nThese notes cover the fundamentals of complex numbers, their representation, and operations, including multiplication, division, exponentiation, and root extraction in polar form.\n\n---\n\n## \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#a883e8\"\u003eIntroduction to Complex Numbers\u003c/span\u003e\n\nThe concept of complex numbers arises from the need to solve equations that have no real solutions, such as:\n\n$$\nx^2 + 1 \u003d 0 \\implies x^2 \u003d -1\n$$\n\nIn the set of real numbers, $\\mathbb{R}$, there is no number whose square is negative. To solve this, we introduce the **imaginary unit**, denoted by $i$.\n\n**Definition: Imaginary Unit**\nThe imaginary unit $i$ is defined as the principal square root of -1.\n$$\ni \u003d \\sqrt{-1} \\quad \\text{such that} \\quad i^2 \u003d -1\n$$\nThis allows us to define the set of [[Complex Numbers]].\n\nA complex number, typically denoted by $z$, is an expression of the form:\n$$\nz \u003d a + ib\n$$\nwhere $a$ and $b$ are real numbers.\n-   $a \u003d \\text{Re}(z)$ is the **real part** of $z$.\n-   $b \u003d \\text{Im}(z)$ is the **imaginary part** of $z$.\n\nThe set of all complex numbers is denoted by $\\mathbb{C}$. This can also be viewed as the set of all ordered pairs $(a, b)$ where $a, b \\in \\mathbb{R}$, which corresponds to the Cartesian product $\\mathbb{R} \\times \\mathbb{R}$.\n\n---\n\n## \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#a883e8\"\u003e[[Algebraic Properties of Complex Numbers]]\u003c/span\u003e\n\nComplex numbers follow specific rules for arithmetic operations.\n\n### \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#8ab4f8\"\u003eAddition and Subtraction\u003c/span\u003e\n\nGiven two complex numbers $z \u003d a + ib$ and $w \u003d c + id$:\n$$\nz + w \u003d (a+c) + i(b+d)\n$$\n$$\nz - w \u003d (a-c) + i(b-d)\n$$\nAddition is performed by adding the real and imaginary parts separately.\n\n### \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#8ab4f8\"\u003eMultiplication\u003c/span\u003e\n\nMultiplication is performed by treating the complex numbers as binomials and remembering that $i^2 \u003d -1$:\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nz \\cdot w \u0026\u003d (a+ib)(c+id) \\\\\n\u0026\u003d ac + iad + ibc + i^2bd \\\\\n\u0026\u003d ac + i(ad+bc) - bd \\\\\n\u0026\u003d (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc)\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n### \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#8ab4f8\"\u003eComplex Conjugate\u003c/span\u003e\n\nThe **conjugate** of a complex number $z \u003d a + ib$ is denoted by $\\bar{z}$ and is defined as:\n$$\n\\bar{z} \u003d a - ib\n$$\nGeometrically, it is the reflection of the point $(a, b)$ across the real axis.\n\n### \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#8ab4f8\"\u003eAbsolute Value (Modulus)\u003c/span\u003e\n\nThe **absolute value** or **modulus** of a complex number $z$ is its distance from the origin in the complex plane. It is calculated as:\n$$\n|z| \u003d \\sqrt{z \\cdot \\bar{z}} \u003d \\sqrt{(a+ib)(a-ib)} \u003d \\sqrt{a^2 - (ib)^2} \u003d \\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\n$$\nThe absolute value $|z|$ is always a non-negative real number.\n\n---\n\n## \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#a883e8\"\u003e[[Polar Form of Complex Numbers]]\u003c/span\u003e\n\nWhile the Cartesian form $z \u003d a + ib$ is useful for addition, the **polar form** is ideal for multiplication, division, and finding roots.\n\nA complex number $z \u003d a+ib$ can be represented as a point $(a,b)$ in the complex plane. This point can also be described by its distance from the origin, $r$, and the angle, $\\phi$, it makes with the positive real axis.\n\n-   **Radius (Modulus)**: $r \u003d |z| \u003d \\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$\n-   **Argument (Angle)**: $\\phi \u003d \\arg(z)$, where $\\tan(\\phi) \u003d \\frac{b}{a}$.\n\nFrom trigonometry, we have:\n-   $a \u003d r \\cos(\\phi)$\n-   $b \u003d r \\sin(\\phi)$\n\nSubstituting these into the Cartesian form gives the **polar form**:\n$$\nz \u003d r \\cos(\\phi) + i r \\sin(\\phi) \u003d r(\\cos(\\phi) + i \\sin(\\phi))\n$$\n\n### \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#8ab4f8\"\u003eCritical Analysis: Finding the Correct Angle $\\phi$\u003c/span\u003e\n\nA common mistake is to simply use $\\phi \u003d \\arctan(\\frac{b}{a})$. The arctan function only returns values in $(-\\frac{\\pi}{2}, \\frac{\\pi}{2})$ (or $-90^\\circ$ to $90^\\circ$), which covers Quadrants I and IV. You must check the signs of $a$ and $b$ to determine the correct quadrant and adjust the angle accordingly.\n\n**Example from Notes:** $z \u003d -1 - i$\n\n1.  **Calculate r:** $a\u003d-1$, $b\u003d-1$.\n    $$\n    r \u003d \\sqrt{(-1)^2 + (-1)^2} \u003d \\sqrt{1+1} \u003d \\sqrt{2}\n    $$\n2.  **Calculate tan($\\phi$):**\n    $$\n    \\tan(\\phi) \u003d \\frac{b}{a} \u003d \\frac{-1}{-1} \u003d 1\n    $$\n3.  **Determine Quadrant:** Since both $a$ and $b$ are negative, the point $(-1, -1)$ lies in **Quadrant III**.\n4.  **Find Correct Angle:** The reference angle for $\\tan(\\phi\u0027) \u003d 1$ is $45^\\circ$ or $\\frac{\\pi}{4}$. For Quadrant III, the correct angle is:\n    $$\n    \\phi \u003d 180^\\circ + 45^\\circ \u003d 225^\\circ\n    $$\n    In radians:\n    $$\n    \\phi \u003d \\pi + \\frac{\\pi}{4} \u003d \\frac{5\\pi}{4}\n    $$\n    *Note: Your handwritten note initially had `3π/4`, which would be in Quadrant II. This is a crucial distinction.*\n\nTherefore, the correct polar form is:\n$$\nz \u003d \\sqrt{2} \\left(\\cos(225^\\circ) + i \\sin(225^\\circ)\\right) \\quad \\text{or} \\quad z \u003d \\sqrt{2} \\left(\\cos\\left(\\frac{5\\pi}{4}\\right) + i \\sin\\left(\\frac{5\\pi}{4}\\right)\\right)\n$$\n",

        "text": "2} \u003d \\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\n$$\nThe absolute value $|z|$ is always"
      }, {
        "text": " a non-negative real number.\n\n---\n\n## \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#a883e8\"\u003e"
      }, {
        "text": "[[Polar Form of Complex Numbers]]\u003c/span\u003e\n\nWhile the Cartesian form $z \u003d a + ib$ is useful for addition"
      }, {
        "text": ", the **polar form** is ideal for multiplication, division, and finding roots.\n\nA complex number $z \u003d"
      }, {
        "text": " a+ib$ can be represented as a point $(a,b)$ in the complex plane. This point can also be"
      }, {
        "text": " described by its distance from the origin, $r$, and the angle, $\\phi$, it makes with the positive real axis.\n\n"
      }, {
        "text": "-   **Radius (Modulus)**: $r \u003d |z| \u003d \\sqrt{a^2 + b^"
      }, {
        "text": "2}$\n-   **Argument (Angle)**: $\\phi \u003d \\arg(z)$, where $\\tan(\\phi"
      }, {
        "text": ") \u003d \\frac{b}{a}$.\n\nFrom trigonometry, we have:\n-   $a \u003d r \\"
      }, {
        "text": "cos(\\phi)$\n-   $b \u003d r \\sin(\\phi)$\n\nSubstituting these into the Cartesian form gives"
      }, {
        "text": " the **polar form**:\n$$\nz \u003d r \\cos(\\phi) + i r \\sin(\\phi) \u003d r(\\"
      }, {
        "text": "cos(\\phi) + i \\sin(\\phi))\n$$\n\n### \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#8ab4"
      }, {
        "text": "f8\"\u003eCritical Analysis: Finding the Correct Angle $\\phi$\u003c/span\u003e\n\nA common mistake is to simply use $\\phi \u003d \\arctan"
      }, {
        "text": "(\\frac{b}{a})$. The arctan function only returns values in $(-\\frac{\\pi}{2}, \\frac{\\"
      }, {
        "text": "pi}{2})$ (or $-90^\\circ$ to $90^\\circ$), which covers Quadrants I and"
      }, {
        "text": " IV. You must check the signs of $a$ and $b$ to determine the correct quadrant and adjust the angle accordingly."
      }, {
        "text": "\n\n**Example from Notes:** $z \u003d -1 - i$\n\n1.  **Calculate r:** $a"
      }, {
        "text": "\u003d-1$, $b\u003d-1$.\n    $$\n    r \u003d \\sqrt{(-1)^2 + (-1)^"
      }, {
        "text": "2} \u003d \\sqrt{1+1} \u003d \\sqrt{2}\n    $$\n2.  **"
      }, {
        "text": "Calculate tan($\\phi$):**\n    $$\n    \\tan(\\phi) \u003d \\frac{b}{a} \u003d"
      }, {
        "text": " \\frac{-1}{-1} \u003d 1\n    $$\n3.  **Determine Quadrant:** Since both"
      }, {
        "text": " $a$ and $b$ are negative, the point $(-1, -1)$ lies in **Quadrant III**.\n"
      }, {
        "text": "4.  **Find Correct Angle:** The reference angle for $\\tan(\\phi\u0027) \u003d 1$ is $45^\\circ"
      }, {
        "text": "$ or $\\frac{\\pi}{4}$. For Quadrant III, the correct angle is:\n    $$\n    "
      }, {
        "text": "\\phi \u003d 180^\\circ + 45^\\circ \u003d 225^\\circ\n    $$\n    "
      }, {
        "text": "In radians:\n    $$\n    \\phi \u003d \\pi + \\frac{\\pi}{4} \u003d \\frac{5\\"
      }, {
        "text": "pi}{4}\n    $$\n    *Note: Your handwritten note initially had `3π/4`, which would"
      }, {
        "text": " be in Quadrant II. This is a crucial distinction.*\n\nTherefore, the correct polar form is:\n$$\nz \u003d"
      }, {
        "text": " \\sqrt{2} \\left(\\cos(225^\\circ) + i \\sin(225^\\circ"
      }, {
        "text": ")\\right) \\quad \\text{or} \\quad z \u003d \\sqrt{2} \\left(\\cos\\"
      }, {
        "text": "left(\\frac{5\\pi}{4}\\right) + i \\sin\\left(\\frac{5\\pi"
      }, {
        "text": "}{4}\\right)\\right)\n$$\n"
      }]

      "text": "### \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#8ab4f8\"\u003eOperations in Polar Form\u003c/span\u003e\n\nLet $z_1 \u003d r_1(\\cos(\\phi_1) + i\\sin(\\phi_1))$ and $z_2 \u003d r_2(\\cos(\\phi_2) + i\\sin(\\phi_2))$.\n\n-   **Multiplication:** Multiply the moduli and add the arguments.\n    $$\n    z_1 \\cdot z_2 \u003d r_1 r_2 (\\cos(\\phi_1 + \\phi_2) + i\\sin(\\phi_1 + \\phi_2))\n    $$\n-   **Division:** Divide the moduli and subtract the arguments.\n    $$\n    \\frac{z_1}{z_2} \u003d \\frac{r_1}{r_2} (\\cos(\\phi_1 - \\phi_2) + i\\sin(\\phi_1 - \\phi_2))\n    $$\n\n---\n\n## \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#a883e8\"\u003e[[De Moivre\u0027s Formula]]\u003c/span\u003e\n\nA direct consequence of the multiplication rule is De Moivre\u0027s formula, which provides a simple way to calculate powers of complex numbers.\n\nFor any integer $n$ and complex number $z \u003d r(\\cos(\\phi) + i\\sin(\\phi))$:\n$$\nz^n \u003d r^n(\\cos(n\\phi) + i\\sin(n\\phi))\n$$\n**Justification:** This can be proven by mathematical induction. The base case ($n\u003d2$) is just the multiplication rule. The inductive step assumes the formula holds for $n$ and proves it for $n+1$ by multiplying $z^n$ by $z$.\n\n---\n\n## \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#a883e8\"\u003e[[Roots of Complex Numbers]]\u003c/span\u003e\n\nFinding the $n$-th root of a complex number is where the polar form truly shines. An $n$-th root of $z$ is a complex number $u$ such that $u^n \u003d z$.\n\nUnlike real numbers, a complex number has exactly $n$ distinct $n$-th roots.\n\n**Formula for n-th Roots:**\nGiven $z \u003d r(\\cos(\\phi) + i\\sin(\\phi))$, its $n$ distinct $n$-th roots, $z_k$, are given by:\n$$\nz_k \u003d \\sqrt[n]{r} \\left( \\cos\\left(\\frac{\\phi + 2\\pi k}{n}\\right) + i \\sin\\left(\\frac{\\phi + 2\\pi k}{n}\\right) \\right)\n$$\nfor $k \u003d 0, 1, 2, \\dots, n-1$.\n\n**Justification:**\n-   The $\\sqrt[n]{r}$ part is straightforward.\n-   The angle is divided by $n$ due to De Moivre\u0027s formula.\n-   The term $2\\pi k$ (or $360^\\circ k$) is added because angles are periodic. Adding a full circle ($2\\pi$ or $360^\\circ$) doesn\u0027t change the complex number $z$, but when we divide by $n$, it yields different angles for the roots.\n-   We only need $k$ from $0$ to $n-1$. For $k\u003dn$, the angle becomes $(\\phi + 2\\pi n)/n \u003d \\phi/n + 2\\pi$, which is the same as the angle for $k\u003d0$. The cycle repeats.\n\n### \u003cspan style\u003d\"color:#8ab4f8\"\u003eExample from Notes: Find the 4th roots of $z \u003d -8 + i8\\sqrt{3}$\u003c/span\u003e\n\n**1. Convert to Polar Form:**\n-   **Modulus (r):**\n    $$\n    r \u003d \\sqrt{(-8)^2 + (8\\sqrt{3})^2} \u003d \\sqrt{64 + 64 \\cdot 3} \u003d \\sqrt{64(1+3)} \u003d \\sqrt{256} \u003d 16\n    $$\n-   **Argument ($\\phi$):**\n    -   $a \u003d -8$ (negative), $b \u003d 8\\sqrt{3}$ (positive) $\\implies$ **Quadrant II**.\n    -   $\\tan(\\phi) \u003d \\frac{8\\sqrt{3}}{-8} \u003d -\\sqrt{3}$.\n    -   The reference angle is $60^\\circ$. In Quadrant II, this is $\\phi \u003d 180^\\circ - 60^\\circ \u003d 120^\\circ$.\n\nSo, $z \u003d 16(\\cos(120^\\circ) + i\\sin(120^\\circ))$.\n\n**2. Apply the Root Formula:**\nHere, $n\u003d4$. The roots $z_k$ are:\n$$\nz_k \u003d \\sqrt{16} \\left( \\cos\\left(\\frac{120^\\circ + 360^\\circ k}{4}\\right) + i \\sin\\left(\\frac{120^\\circ + 360^\\circ k}{4}\\right) \\right)\n$$\n$$\nz_k \u003d 2 \\left( \\cos(30^\\circ + 90^\\circ k) + i \\sin(30^\\circ + 90^\\circ k) \\right) \\quad \\text{for } k \u003d 0, 1, 2, 3\n$$\n\n**3. Calculate the Four Roots:**\n-   **k \u003d 0:**\n    $z_0 \u003d 2(\\cos(30^\\circ) + i\\sin(30^\\circ)) \u003d 2\\left(\\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{2} + i\\frac{1}{2}\\right) \u003d \\sqrt{3} + i$\n-   **k \u003d 1:**\n    $z_1 \u003d 2(\\cos(120^\\circ) + i\\sin(120^\\circ)) \u003d 2\\left(-\\frac{1}{2} + i\\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}\\right) \u003d -1 + i\\sqrt{3}$\n-   **k \u003d 2:**\n    $z_2 \u003d 2(\\cos(210^\\circ) + i\\sin(210^\\circ)) \u003d 2\\left(-\\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{2} - i\\frac{1}{2}\\right) \u003d -\\sqrt{3} - i$\n-   **k \u003d 3:**\n    $z_3 \u003d 2(\\cos(300^\\circ) + i\\sin(300^\\circ)) \u003d 2\\left(\\frac{1}{2} - i\\frac{\\sqrt{3}}{2}\\right) \u003d 1 - i\\sqrt{3}$\n\n**4. Geometric Interpretation:**\nThe four roots are equally spaced on a circle of radius 2. They form the vertices of a square.\n\n",
